Stopping Path of a Sequential Procedure for Data in Hand

Source: R/seq_path.R
seq_path.Rd

Applies a sequential check function to data already collected, at each successive sample size, and returns the whole path in one object: the estimate, its confidence limits, the criterion sample size, and the stopping decision at every stage, together with the first sample size at which the stopping rule is met. One call replaces the collect and check loop that would otherwise be written by hand, and the plot() method draws the picture a preregistration or a methods section needs.

Usage

seq_path(check, data, ..., start = NULL, by = 1L)

Arguments

check

A sequential check function: any function that returns a sequential check object (class "smsd_check"), such as seq_aipe_cv, seq_aipe_smd, seq_aipe_r, or seq_mr_cv.

data

The data collected so far, in the order collected: a vector, a list with one element for each data argument of check, or a data frame whose columns are named after those arguments. See Supplying the Data.

...

The other arguments of check, passed unchanged and whole at every stage (for example width and conf_level, or A and c). Data do not belong here: an argument that looks like data is refused unless it is wrapped in I() (see Supplying the Data). seq_path() matches its own arguments check and data by exact name or by position only, so an argument such as c = 75 or d = 0.5 reaches the check function and is not taken, by partial matching, for check or data.

start

The first sample size checked. NULL (the default) is the procedure's pilot sample size when check is one of this package's check functions, and the smallest sample size check accepts otherwise. Other choices: a single whole number; a pilot function (called with those arguments in ... that it shares with check); "pilot" (the package's pilot function for check; an error if there is none); or "earliest" (the smallest sample size check accepts). See Where the Path Starts.

by

The number of observations (per data element) added between checks. The default, 1, is the purely sequential procedure of the cited articles. A larger value shows what a study that checks after every batch of by observations would have seen; observations beyond the last complete batch are not used.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_path", "data.frame") with one row per stage and the columns

n

the number of observations taken from each data element at this stage (integer).

estimate

the point estimate.

lower_limit, upper_limit

the confidence limits (NA for the risk based procedures, which have no interval).

current_n

the sample size as check reports it.

criterion_n

the criterion sample size at this stage (NA for a procedure that has none).

is_satisfied

whether the stopping rule is met at this stage.

variance_unusable

whether the variance estimate was zero, negative, or not finite at this stage. No variance has then been estimated, and the check functions report the stopping rule as not met, whatever the other columns show (see smsd_check_methods): the criterion sample size and any confidence limits in that row rest on no estimated variance. NA when check does not report it.

The attributes are stop_n (the first n at which the rule is met; NA if it is never met), method, estimate_term (the name of the quantity estimated), conf_level and width (absent for procedures without them), start (the first sample size checked), start_rule (how it was chosen: "pilot", "earliest", or "supplied"), by, n_observations (the number of observations in hand per data element), arguments (the list passed through ..., as check received it), and final_check: the smsd_check object at stop_n or, when the rule is never met, at the last stage. Stored values are never rounded. A warning that check gives at several stages is reported once, with the number of stages.

What the Path Shows, and What It Does Not

The path shows what the stopping rule would have said at each sample size for these data in this order. A sequential design decides at each stage from the observations collected so far, without looking ahead: it stops at the first sample size at which the rule is met, and the estimate and interval it reports are the ones at that sample size (stop_n), not at a later, more favorable one. The rows after stop_n are shown for illustration only. Choosing a later stage because its estimate or interval looks better is not the sequential procedure, and the properties the procedure was derived to have (the width and coverage of the interval, or the risk) do not hold for an estimate chosen that way. For the same reason the observations must be in the order in which they were, or will be, collected.

Supplying the Data

At each stage data is cut to its first \(n\) observations and passed to check.

  • A vector is passed as the first argument of check (the one sample procedures).

  • A list holds one element for each data argument of check: either named after those arguments, as in list(group_1 = a, group_2 = b) for two independent groups or list(x = x, y = y) for a predictor and a response, or unnamed and in the order check expects them (the help page of each check function gives the names of its data arguments). Each element is a vector, a matrix or data frame whose rows are observations, or a list of these (for example the groups of seq_aipe_c), every member of which is cut to its first \(n\) observations.

  • A data frame is read as a named list of its columns, so the column names must be argument names of check.

Every element must hold the same number of observations, because stage \(n\) uses the first \(n\) of each: \(n\) is the sample size for one sample procedures, the per group sample size for group designs, and the number of pairs for paired data. The column current_n gives the sample size on the scale check itself reports (for example the total over both groups for seq_mr_smd), which is the scale of criterion_n.

All of the data go in data. Only data is cut to its first \(n\) observations; everything in ... is passed whole at every stage. A second group or a second variable written after data (for example the second group in seq_path(seq_mr_smd, group_1, group_2, ...)) would therefore be seen in full from the first stage on, which is the looking ahead a sequential design rules out. seq_path() stops with a message when an argument in ... looks like data: it holds two or more observations and check still runs when it is cut along with data. In the rare case that such an argument really is not data, wrap it in I() to pass it whole.

Missing values are refused. The path is indexed by the number of observations collected, and several check functions drop missing values by default (the minimum risk, bounded risk, fixed width, and bounded length functions, whose na.rm is TRUE unless set otherwise; the seq_aipe_* functions stop on a missing value), so with missing values the sample size a stage reports would be smaller than the stage and the first check would come before the pilot sample size had been reached. Remove the incomplete observations first (both members of a pair, the whole row of a matrix or data frame), and trim the elements to a common length if they then differ.

Where the Path Starts

A sequential procedure begins checking at its pilot sample size, not before, and the path does the same. By default (start = NULL) the first stage is the procedure's pilot sample size whenever check is one of this package's check functions: its _pilot companion (for example seq_aipe_cv_pilot for seq_aipe_cv) is called with those arguments in ... that it shares with check, and with its own defaults for the rest. For any other function (a wrapper, or a check function of the user's own) the default is the smallest sample size the function accepts, found by trying. start can also be given as a number, as a pilot function, or as "earliest" to see the rule from the smallest sample size the check accepts. A pilot function that needs an argument check does not take (the minimum pilot sample size m_0, for example, or a number of predictors) cannot be given that argument through ...: call the pilot function yourself and pass the number it returns as start.

Where the path starts can change where it stops. The stopping rules of seq_aipe_cv, seq_aipe_sm, seq_aipe_smd, seq_aipe_r, seq_aipe_reg_coef, seq_aipe_c, seq_aipe_gini, seq_mr_cv, and seq_mr_smd (with one sampling cost) contain a correction term that keeps the rule from being met below the sample size the pilot formula gives. The pilot sample size is the larger of that and a minimum (4 by default), so for these procedures an earlier start can change stop_n only when the target is so loose that the formula gives less than the minimum, and then only if the check function accepts fewer observations than the minimum. Several of the classical procedures (for example the fixed width, minimum risk, and bounded risk procedures for a normal mean) have no correction term at all: started below the pilot, their rule can be met by chance at a very small sample size, which is not a sample size at which the procedure itself would have stopped. If a study used a pilot sample size other than the default (a larger minimum, for example), supply that number.

Procedures That Do Not Fit

The two stage procedures (ts_*) take one pilot sample and one further sample whose size the pilot determines, so they have no stage by stage path: call the ts_* function once on the pilot sample to learn the total sample size required, and once more when the additional observations are in. The budget constrained procedure (seq_budget) allocates observations unequally across groups according to their costs and variances, so its path is not indexed by one common sample size: call seq_budget() after each new observation. The minimum risk procedure for the standardized mean difference with two costs (seq_mr_smd with c = c(c1, c2)) is refused for the same reason: its pilot returns one size per group. seq_path() stops with a message saying so when given one of these.

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2019). Sequential accuracy in parameter estimation for population correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 24(4), 492–515. doi:10.1037/met0000203

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

See also

plot.smsd_path for the plot, smsd_path_methods for the other methods, and seq_report for a sentence that reports the result.

Other seq_path: plot.smsd_path(), smsd_path_methods

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

set.seed(113)
# Response times (seconds) of 120 participants, in the order tested. At
# what sample size does a 95% confidence interval of full width 0.10 for
# the coefficient of variation first meet the stopping rule?
response_time <- rgamma(120, shape = 16, rate = 20)
path <- seq_path(seq_aipe_cv, response_time, width = 0.10)
path
#> Sequential path: coefficient of variation
#> 
#>   Stages checked  : 81 (n = 40 to 120)
#>   First check at  : the pilot sample size
#>   Target width    : 0.1
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Rule first met  : n = 61
#>   Estimate there  : cv = 0.2530166 [0.2152415, 0.2907917]
#> 
#>     n   estimate  lower_limit  upper_limit  criterion_n  is_satisfied
#>    40  0.2322022    0.1843518    0.2800525           76         FALSE
#>    41  0.2332873    0.1859133    0.2806612           75         FALSE
#>    42  0.2326324    0.1873538    0.2779110           72         FALSE
#>   ...
#>   118  0.2503885    0.2223552    0.2784219           51          TRUE
#>   119  0.2504532    0.2228470    0.2780593           50          TRUE
#>   120  0.2493359    0.2217831    0.2768887           50          TRUE
#> 
#>   The estimate to report is the one at n = 61. Later rows show what the
#>   rule would have said had sampling continued; they are not grounds for
#>   choosing a different stopping point.
attr(path, "stop_n")
#> [1] 61

# Engagement after a training program against a control group, checked
# after every 10 participants per group. This study's pilot was 20 per
# group, larger than the default pilot, so it is supplied.
trained <- rnorm(120, mean = 4.8, sd = 0.9)
control <- rnorm(120, mean = 4.5, sd = 0.9)
seq_path(seq_aipe_smd, list(group_1 = trained, group_2 = control),
         width = 0.60, start = 20, by = 10)
#> Sequential path: standardized mean difference
#> 
#>   Stages checked  : 11 (n = 20 to 120 by 10)
#>   First check at  : the sample size supplied as 'start'
#>   Target width    : 0.6
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Rule first met  : n = 100
#>   Estimate there  : smd = 0.4527979 [0.1591645, 0.7464314]
#> 
#>     n   estimate  lower_limit  upper_limit  criterion_n  is_satisfied
#>    20  0.2513720  -0.37484398    0.8775880           90         FALSE
#>    30  0.5121502  -0.02351928    1.0478197           98         FALSE
#>    40  0.4407556  -0.01942790    0.9009391           96         FALSE
#>   ...
#>   100  0.4527979   0.15916448    0.7464314           97          TRUE
#>   110  0.4843968   0.20437793    0.7644156           97          TRUE
#>   120  0.4383967   0.17313872    0.7036547           95          TRUE
#> 
#>   The estimate to report is the one at n = 100. Later rows show what
#>   the rule would have said had sampling continued; they are not grounds
#>   for choosing a different stopping point.

# A minimum risk procedure: the loss constant A and the unit cost c
# replace the width and the confidence level.
seq_path(seq_mr_cv, response_time, A = 400000, c = 75)
#> Sequential path: minimum risk point estimation (coefficient of variation)
#> 
#>   Stages checked  : 103 (n = 18 to 120)
#>   First check at  : the pilot sample size
#>   Arguments       : A = 400000, c = 75
#>   Rule first met  : n = 20
#>   Estimate there  : cv = 0.2195011
#> 
#>     n   estimate  criterion_n  is_satisfied
#>    18  0.2274672           20         FALSE
#>    19  0.2230411           20         FALSE
#>    20  0.2195011           20          TRUE
#>   ...
#>   118  0.2503885           14          TRUE
#>   119  0.2504532           14          TRUE
#>   120  0.2493359           14          TRUE
#> 
#>   The estimate to report is the one at n = 20. Later rows show what the
#>   rule would have said had sampling continued; they are not grounds for
#>   choosing a different stopping point.
